name: Esther Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Esther. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a studio of four that does branding for small firms: two dental practices, a vet clinic, a couple of tech start-ups that may or may not survive. I set up most of our AI workflows, so my mornings are often generating logo directions and mock-ups, and my afternoons are cleaning them up and presenting. In the evenings I run a little online shop selling wedding invitation templates. My partner Joel teaches at the primary school down the road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving the puzzle of what a business actually is, and then showing it back to them. The vet clinic cried when they saw their new sign, in a good way. What wears me out is the pay, honestly, and how every invoice from a start-up arrives two months late. We've got about three weeks of money in the bank, which is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a good tool and that's all, let's get back to work. I'd probably post a few tips on what actually saves time. Nothing dramatic either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a bit of a relief, but my real worries are still there. Our pay is low, and the start-ups pay late, which means some months the studio is tight. If one start-up folds owing us money, that's my bonus gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and push the studio to take more steady clients, like dentists, who pay on time. I'd grow the invitation shop, maybe to two hundred a month. And I'd build a one-month cushion by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine, but the money around it is wobbly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your income does the invitation shop bring in now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eighty a month in a good month, more in spring when people book weddings. It's small, but it's the difference between saving and not. I'd love to double it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the late payments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody really, it's how small businesses work. Everyone's waiting on someone else. I'd just want the studio to stop taking clients who can't pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but kindly. I'd offer to show other designers what I've learned. Online I'd post honest notes about what works and what doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm fine at first, because I'm the one who set up the tools. But the studio will need fewer people. And clients will start asking why they're paying studio prices for something that took an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ines, who owns the studio, to let me run a package for small clients: a full brand in a week, built with AI, at a lower price. I'd automate the invitation shop so customers can personalise templates themselves. And I'd learn to direct photo shoots, because clients still need real pictures of real staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I like a challenge. It feels like the ground shifting under a game I know how to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If clients ask why they're paying for an hour's work, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they're paying for knowing which of the hundred options is right. And for someone who'll answer the phone when the sign is the wrong size. Whether they'll keep paying for that, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the studio would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben, our junior, who mostly does resizing and social posts. That's the first thing that goes. I'd try to teach him the tools before Ines decides anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's arrived and there's no point pretending otherwise. I'd want the government to sort out support for people losing work, quickly. I'd say that plainly online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my design job is over within a year. Branding is thinking work, and it all goes on day one. Being good with the AI tools only buys me a few months when AGI arrives in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into wedding and event photography straight away, since I already know the wedding market from the shop. Photography is hands-on, so it lasts until the robots, around 2031. I'd borrow a camera from my cousin and do three weddings at cost to build a portfolio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually quick, but two years is too quick even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three weddings at cost with three weeks of savings. How would you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel's wage would cover rent for a while, and teaching probably lasts longer than design. I'd sell my second monitor and the good chair. And I'd keep the invitation shop running until it stops selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 2031 look like for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe photography goes too, maybe people still want a person at their wedding. I'd hope for the second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to make a proper plan, and I'd share mine openly. People in design need to look at the hands-on side of creative work. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is quite good for me. I could build a photography side business while still earning from design. By 2031 I'd want photography to be most of my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy a second-hand camera, about six hundred, paid off over a year. I'd shoot weekends and keep the studio job. And I'd use AI to run the admin, bookings and editing so I can take more jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I'd be tired, not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't editing photos with AI part of what will replace you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd use it anyway. The bit people pay for is me being there on the day, knowing when the bride's dad is about to cry. I'd let the software do the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Joel change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd hold off on a bigger flat for a couple of years. Get the photography going first. Then maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's use it well. I'd tell friends to keep learning. I'd stay upbeat in public, because I honestly would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years lets me ride the design wave for a while and move on my own terms. I'd make the most of being good with the tools now. Then I'd move into photography and events gradually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask Ines for a raise, given how much faster I've made the studio. I'd grow the invitation shop and start a few small photo jobs. And I'd save two months of costs by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It feels like a long game I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a long game. What could make you lose it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. If I stay at the studio until 2034 because it's easy, I'd be too late. I'd want a date in my calendar to check myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans with Joel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd buy somewhere small in four or five years. Teaching and photography together feel steadier than design alone. We'd want kids around thirty-two.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even being quick doesn't help in two years. What would help is help with starting small businesses, like cheap loans for equipment, and short courses in hands-on creative work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what is left of the job. I keep asking myself what people will still pay a person for. I think it's being there, in the room, on the day.

portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old designer** who set up her studio's **AI workflows**.
She runs a small **invitation shop** on the side, the gap between saving and not.
She's **pragmatic** and doesn't blame anyone, focusing on what still needs a person.
Across the pictures, she plans a move into **wedding photography** and events.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even being quick doesn't help in two years.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **equipment loans** and short courses in **hands-on** creative work.
